1: Welcome to Part 1 of the implementation series for H R-driven identity.
The H R pipeline makes an account exist.
This guide makes the H R record decide everything that happens to that account afterward, and proves it did.
It does that in seven gates.

For each gate, we'll cover what done means, the steps, the commands from the developer workbook's first lab, the federal requirement and the evidence an I S S O keeps, what's available in G C C and G C C High, and how to roll it back.
Part 1 takes the first three gates: one writer for every account state, employees and contractors from their sources, and joiners ready on day one.
Design guidance is labeled, and the workbook's code is illustrative, tested against fixtures rather than a lyve tenant.
2: Here are all seven gates on one page.
The first is done when every account state and H R attribute has exactly one recorded writer, and the other write paths are gone.
The second is done when employees come from H R, and contractors come from a named source with an enforced end date.
The third is done when the pre-hire and day-one workflows run with limits, and day-one readiness is measured.

Part 2 picks up from there: access assigned from attributes, with a review of what a move leaves behind; piv and CAC credentials tied to H R events; separations that block access first and dispose of the account last; and drift found and closed at the source.
Each gate names the validation kit checks that prove part of it, and says plainly where no check exists yet.
Every threshold is a proposed starting point the agency approves or replaces.
3: The gates assume some things are already in place.
The H R pipeline is lyve, with shadow differences explained and no unmatched creations.
The attribute foundation is done: the slot register is signed, and the attributes are proven on the pilot.
The Federal Modernization Workbook's Book 03's first-phase decisions are made: the person key, the authority map, the worker types and the privacy basis.
Inbound provisioning needs Entra I D P1, but workflows, entitlement management, access reviews and automatic assignment need Entra I D Governance.
Roles go through pim, with the workflows administrator role behind approval.
And logs leave Entra I D before the first gate, because its own retention is short and can't be recovered later.
As for where things run: the H R platform runs on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and the lifecycle's automation runs in Azure.
Apps on AWS or Oracle Cloud only see these changes through the access Entra I D grants them.
4: The first gate starts from one idea.
Whoever can write an attribute effectively decides any access that a rule grants from it.
Account state works the same way, and two systems can set it: the pipeline, and Lifecycle Workflows.
So the register gets a row for every transition, each with one writer and one backstop.
Inbound provisioning creates the account, and nothing else does.
At hire, pick one writer to enable the account, either the pipeline or the day-one workflow, and record the other as the backstop.
At separation, the pipeline disables the account before the leaver workflow first runs.
Only the pipeline can re-enable a cancelled separation.
Deletion belongs to a separate post-separation workflow, never to a bulk upload.
The hire and leave dates, and the manager, are written only by provisioning.
H R, not IT, records a new supervisor.
And the certificate binding belongs to the card system.
5: Three more steps finish the first gate.
First, write down which records provision at all, including leave, secondments and pre-hire lookahead, and version that filter.
Remember, someone on leave hasn't left.
Second, remove every other way to write these values: the help desk, self-service, Exchange administrators, and the permissions on Active Directory's organizational units.
One path is easy to miss.
Whoever can write the certificate mapping attribute in A D decides which card can sign in as which synced user.
Third, save an audit query for each protected value, one that finds writes by anyone but the named writer.
Gate seven will run those queries.
The interim path matters for most agencies.
Until A D retires, sync is a writer too, so record the sync agent's managed service account as a writer, and review those permissions every quarter.
6: The workbook's first chapter turns the register into code, and its lab runs on fictional audit records with no tenant.
The check reads the register itself: one writer per row, every required transition present, no deletes by provisioning, and the register signed with its scope versioned.
The program's own register comes back clean.
Then the scan compares a month of audit records with the register.
Five came from the right writer, one from the backstop, four from a second writer, and one from a writer the register forbids.
So a help desk account disabled a leaver, a fix-up script wrote a coded slot, and provisioning deleted an account.
The scan doesn't read Active Directory.
And the audit property names it matches aren't documented by Microsoft, so confirm them in a test tenant before you trust the scan.
7: Here's the federal side of the first gate.
Account management and identifier management are both in the Moderate baseline.
For those, the I S S O keeps the signed register, with its lifecycle rows and its versioned scope filter.
Audit review covers writes made outside the named writer, and the evidence is the saved queries plus the A D auditing settings.
The feed also needs a privacy determination for each flow.
To validate, two kit checks confirm there are no duplicate keys and that the key fields are filled in.
But they measure values, not writers.
Nothing in the kit reads who can write yet.
So the evidence for writers is the delegation export, the permission review, and a clean run of the saved queries over the pilot's last thirty days.
Everything this gate uses is available in both government clouds.
To roll back, make a signed register change.
A removed permission comes back only through a recorded change, with an end date.
8: The second gate brings each population in from its own source.
For employees, the pipeline already exists.
This gate checks one thing: that the feed reads hires and separations by their published date, so the pre-hire and pre-separation workflows have time to run.
Contractors are different, because they aren't in Federal H R 2.0.
The program's decision is an agency-owned contractor system of record for now, with Oracle's contingent worker as a later swap.
Reconcile the contractor register, the card system and the accounts in both directories, read-only, using the person key.
Then settle six questions with the register's owner: who owns it, what's in it, how fresh it is, its privacy basis, the join key, and its coverage.
Contractors map into the same record, with their own worker type code, the sponsor as manager, and their own provisioning app.
The contractor piv path is still pending proof.
9: For contractors, ship the leaver before the joiner.
An end date in a spreadsheet that nobody updates keeps access alive.
So the middleware works out the earliest end.
That's the contract end, capped by the completion date; suitability withdrawn; the card terminated; the sponsor gone past a grace period; or a missed sponsor recertification.
Whichever comes first, the middleware sends the leave date and disables the account itself.
The table comes from the workbook's lab.
Four fictional contractors go inactive, each for a different reason.
One of them had a card expiring in late October, but a recertification that came due earlier, so the earlier date wins.
Two records are quarantined, one with no contract end and one with a sponsor H R doesn't know.
Sponsors recertify through a twice-yearly access review.
Here's the design choice: if the sponsor doesn't respond, access is removed.
10: The workbook's second chapter builds this in code, reusing the H R middleware that already exists.
The extract step takes nine fictional records and finds three active, four past their earliest end, and two quarantined.
Every record carries its end date, so the leaver workflow fires on the right day.
The middleware turns that extract into one batch of seven requests, including four disables.
Nothing is sent, because a dry run is its default.
Then the read-only reconciliation finds seven issues.
Four are accounts still enabled past their earliest end, and they're exactly the four disables waiting to go.
The others are an orphan account, a card for someone the source doesn't know, and a leave date that would fire on the wrong day.
Finally, the review step writes the sponsor review settings.
Once the disables go out, the next reconciliation is clean.
That clean re-run is the evidence for the gate.
11: On the federal side, account management and external personnel security call for the source decision, the reconciliation report, and how long each contractor's access took to block after their end date.
Identifying each person by status means the worker type code appears on every account.
O M B's zero trust memo says enterprise identity draws on H R, contract management and personnel security, so the governance body signs a table that names one authority for each fact.
To validate, one kit check lists enabled accounts with no key, which is where contractors without one show up.
No check reads end dates, so the evidence is the reconciliation re-run, with no contractor past their end.
In Azure Government, A P I-driven inbound provisioning and access reviews are available.
Until the contractor source is automated, keep the contract end date as the leave date so the leaver still fires.
To roll back, pause the contractor app.
12: The third gate makes joiners ready on day one.
The account already exists, disabled, because the pipeline sent it early.
Build just a few workflows: pre-hire, day-one, mover, leaver, post-leaver, and the rehire and conversion workflows.
Scope them by coded attributes, never one per organization.
Microsoft gives two different ceilings for workflows, fifty on one page and a hundred on another, so budget to fifty.
A workflow can hold up to twenty-five tasks.
The tenant schedule runs every three hours by default and can be set anywhere from one to twenty-four.
Every workflow shares it, so set it once, with the leaver in mind.
Set the hire time early in the day.
Give every scheduled workflow an execution limit a little above a normal week, so an anomaly gets quarantined.
In the workbook's files, the day-one workflow doesn't enable the account.
13: A new hire needs a way to sign in before their card arrives.
The pre-hire workflow has a built-in task that creates a Temporary Access Pass and emails it to the manager.
It starts on the hire date.
It needs the manager and the manager's email filled in.
And it only works for someone with no other sign-in methods, no earlier sign-ins and no Entra role assignments.
So a rehire who kept their old methods won't qualify, and needs a separate path.
Microsoft recommends a pass sent to a new hire last no more than twenty-four hours, and the tenant can force one-time use.
Day-one access comes from an onboarding package, with department access assigned automatically in gate four.
Never add a new hire straight to an application group.
Then measure the share of hires who are fully ready at the start of day one.
The pass is only a bridge.
Once the card is bound, an account still running on a pass is a finding.
14: The workbook's third chapter keeps the workflows as reviewed files.
Its lint passes the program's six files.

Against three broken copies, it catches an offset outside Microsoft's range, too many workflows for the budget, a missing execution limit, a joiner that adds groups directly, delete and disable in the same workflow, and a pass that lasts three days.
The plan step refuses to run if any file has a finding.
Then it compares each file with the tenant's export.
A missing workflow becomes a create, and a changed one becomes a new version, because workflows are versioned, not edited in place.
It reads with one permission and sends nothing.
Execution limits aren't in the A P I, so record them in the file.
Last, readiness checks each hire for an enabled, licensed account, the onboarding package, and a completed pre-hire run.
One of four fictional hires is ready.
Run it on an export from the start of the day.
15: On the federal side, automated account management calls for the workflow definitions, their versions, and run history exported before Entra's thirty-day view drops it.
Authenticator management requires that the first authenticator is time-limited and goes to an accountable person.
So the I S S O keeps the pass policy and the task's settings.
To validate, one kit check flags hires whose start date has passed with no processing record.
Another confirms execution limits are set, and counts workflows against the ceiling.
Add the run history for the last group of hires, and the readiness rate.
Lifecycle Workflows and entitlement management are available in Azure Government.
But Microsoft's government table has no row for the Temporary Access Pass, so its availability in G C C High isn't confirmed.
Before Governance is licensed, the pipeline enables the account on the hire date and the help desk issues the pass.
To roll back, disable the workflow's schedule.
16: To close Part 1, here's what each gate leaves behind, and where Part 2 picks it up.
The first gate leaves the register, the scope filter and the saved audit queries.
The separation gate relies on its rule that the pipeline disables first, and the drift gate runs its queries.
The second gate leaves the source decisions, the authority table and the reconciliation reports.
The credentials gate reads contractor card events, and the separation gate measures how fast contractors are blocked after their end date.
The third gate leaves the workflows and their run history.
The mover workflow, the end of the pass bridge, and the leaver sequence all build on it.
Part 2 covers access and movers, credentials, separation, and drift and evidence.
To build Part 1's code, use the developer workbook, Building H R-Driven Identity, chapters one to three, each with its labs.
And to learn it in order, use the learning path for H R-driven identity: seven modules, one per gate, each with a fixture lab and a knowledge check.
